title: Senate Sets September 15 Cloture Vote to Take Up the CLARITY Act
description: Senators will vote September 15 on cloture for the motion to proceed to the CLARITY Act. The procedural test does not pass the bill, classify XRP, or change federal law.
author: Jack Nelson
imageAlt: U.S. Capitol at dusk framed by translucent legislative pages and a blue digital-asset network
keyTakeaways: The Senate record confirms a September 15 cloture vote on the motion to proceed to H.R. 3633, the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act.
Cloture would clear only an early 60-vote procedural hurdle. It would not pass the bill, make it law, or complete Senate consideration.
The released Senate text does not name XRP or Ripple, so the scheduled vote does not itself classify XRP or change its legal status.

sections.heading: What is the September 15 vote?
paragraphs: The Senate is scheduled to vote on September 15, 2026, at 2:15 p.m. Eastern Time on cloture for the motion to proceed to H.R. 3633. This is a 60-vote procedural test about whether the chamber should move toward considering the CLARITY Act.

The vote is not final passage. It would not make the bill law, classify XRP, or complete Senate debate. The Senate floor record and Congressional Record confirm the scheduled step; independent reporting confirms that bipartisan support remains uncertain.

sections.heading: What happens if cloture passes?
paragraphs: If at least 60 senators support cloture, debate on the motion to proceed becomes limited under Senate rules. The Senate would still need to approve that motion before formally taking up H.R. 3633.

Consideration could then include debate, amendments, more procedural votes, and a final-passage vote. If the Senate changes the House bill, both chambers must approve identical text before it can go to the president. September 15 is therefore a decision point, not a forecast of enactment.

sections.heading: What would the CLARITY Act change?
paragraphs: The July 22 Senate draft proposes a broad U.S. digital-asset market structure. It would divide responsibilities between the SEC and CFTC and create rules for disclosures, trading platforms, custody, customer assets, anti-money-laundering controls, decentralized finance, and future agency rulemaking.

It is not an XRP-specific bill, and the July draft is not guaranteed to become the operative Senate text. Negotiators can revise it through a substitute, amendments, or a bipartisan agreement. The text placed before senators in September will matter more than earlier summaries.

sections.heading: Does the vote change XRP's legal status?
paragraphs: No. The released draft does not name XRP or Ripple, and a cloture vote does not change federal law. It does not declare XRP a commodity, alter a court ruling, approve a financial product, or support a price prediction.

XRP-related businesses still have a reason to monitor the bill because final rules for exchanges, brokers, custody, disclosures, and customer assets could affect how U.S. intermediaries support digital assets. Any XRP-specific effect would depend on enacted definitions, agency rules, and the facts of a particular transaction or service.

sections.heading: What could still derail or reshape the bill?
paragraphs: The reported disputes include government ethics, illicit-finance and law-enforcement provisions, and stablecoin rewards or yield. Filing cloture reserves a place in the floor process, but it does not prove that leaders have the required 60 votes.

A compromise could add support, while a disputed amendment could cost votes. No public roll call existed when this report was published, so claims about individual senators or the bill's probability of becoming law remain forecasts.

sections.heading: What should XRP readers watch next?
paragraphs: Watch whether cloture reaches 60 votes, which legislative text advances, and whether a revised amendment package changes the rules for intermediaries, disclosures, custody, customer assets, or agency jurisdiction.

Treat procedural headlines as process updates, not legal reclassification or investment signals. The next verifiable milestone is the September 15 vote unless the Senate changes the schedule or negotiators release materially revised text first.

whatToWatch: The September 15, 2026, cloture vote scheduled for 2:15 p.m. Eastern Time, and whether it reaches the 60-vote threshold.
Any revised substitute or amendment package addressing government ethics, illicit finance, law enforcement, or stablecoin rewards before the vote.
Whether the Senate adopts the motion to proceed and later schedules debate, amendments, additional cloture votes, and final passage.
If the Senate passes a different text, whether the House approves identical language before the measure is presented to the president.
Only after enactment, the SEC and CFTC rulemakings, effective dates, and transition provisions that would determine real-world compliance effects.
